items.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I found Capitol records releases “The Best of the Nat King Cole Trio” Part one and two. And I go my God, boom... I learned all the songs. And I said now that, that’s music. That’s something I can do... I just wrapped myself around that.

ctx.x: Wow. Did use of your vocal thing come along naturally. I know I’ve been reading about Nat King Cole who — it was suggested to him like, you need to start singing, or could you, and from there, it’s history.

Well I played in I think it was the beginning of college. Since I was already singing and playing in rock bands through high school, when I went to college I had my guitar and I had with me the Kenny Rankin album, I had some Michael Franks records, and some James Taylor stuff. And I had seen guys who sat and played the guitar, you know, folk guys. And so I learned some of these Kenny Rankin songs, like “Haven’t We Met” and he did “Here’s that Rainy Day,” and he did “Sunny Gets Blue” on this one record. And then I…

minutes and he’d say “sing, sing something.” And he’d say — and I’d do “Straighten Up and Fly Right,” “For Sentimental Reasons.” And then we would close out. We would do an Ellington medley and “Sing Sing Sing” or a little Goodman medley. And so as luck would have it, it’s amazing, it’s weird thinking about it because it’s so long ago to me now. In 1983, in May of ’83 I was singing this tune “I Like Jersey Best.” A buddy of mine wrote this song about our state, make a little rock & roll record with my friend…

items.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I asked about Nat King Cole. Well what did you think? And he went, “well, he was something. He was a good piano player, yeah. And one day he started singing.”

ctx.x: I might be rambling you know. I never am allowed to talk this much. And still I do. But it was one of those things. I mean this song became a sort of little hit, this “I Like Jersey Best” thing and then like a year later Stash said, “let’s make another record.” So I made another record and Dave McKenna was in town. I said, “well let’s get McKenna, and we’ll get Butch Miles and Jerry Bruno played bass, and we did half with them and my dad, some more Nat King Cole things “This Will Make You Laugh,” “Hit That Jive…
Yeah. You’re getting paid to rehearse.
